text:
Botswana - Wikipedia
Contents
Botswana
Botswana
,
[
c
]
officially the
Republic of Botswana
,
[
d
]
is a
landlocked country
in
Southern Africa
. Botswana is topographically flat, with approximately 70% of its territory being a part of the
Kalahari Desert
. It is bordered by
South Africa
to the south and southeast,
Namibia
to the west and north,
Zambia
to the north, and
Zimbabwe
to the northeast. Its total area is
581,730 square kilometres (224,610
sq
mi)
. Gaborone, in the
South-East District
, is the country's capital and largest city.
Botswana is one of the
most sparsely populated
countries in the world. While it is not enshrined by statutory law, Botswana is
de facto
the
nation state
of the
Batswana people
, who constitute nearly 80% of the population while legally undistinguished
Kalanga people
, who account for another 11%, are the single largest ethnic minority.
The Batswana ethnic group are descended mainly from
Bantu-speaking peoples
who
migrated into southern Africa
, including modern Botswana, in several waves before
AD
600. In 1885, the
British
colonised the area and declared a protectorate named
Bechuanaland
. As part of the
decolonisation of Africa
, Bechuanaland became an independent
Commonwealth republic
under its current name on 30 September 1966. Since then, it has been a
parliamentary republic
with a consistent record of uninterrupted democratic
elections
, though
dominated
by the
Botswana Democratic Party
until
2024
, when the
Umbrella for Democratic Change
won the 2024 Botswana general election.
Botswana's economy has generally experienced stable growth since independence. It is dominated by
tourism
and
mining
; Botswana produces more diamonds than any other country. Its
gross national income per capita
(
purchasing power parity
) of about $20,158
as of 2024
[
update
]
(by some estimates the fourth-largest in Africa) gives the country a relatively high
standard of living
and the second-highest
Human Development Index
of continental
sub-Saharan Africa
, after South Africa. Despite Botswana’s economic gains, Botswana continues to grapple with high unemployment, severe income inequality, and one of the world's most
critical HIV/AIDS epidemics
. Botswana is a member of the
Southern African Customs Union
, the
Southern African Development Community
, the
Commonwealth of Nations
and the United Nations.
Etymology
The country's name means "Land of the
Tswana
", referring to the dominant
ethnic group in Botswana
.
[
12
]
[
13
]
The
Constitution of Botswana
recognises a homogeneous Tswana state.
[
14
]
The
demonym
Batswana
was originally applied to the Tswana,
[
15
]
and has also come to be used generally as a term for all citizens of Botswana.
[
16
]
In
Setswana
,
Batswana
is grammatically plural; its singular form, which can refer to a single member of the Tswana or to a single citizen of Botswana, is
Motswana
.
[
15
]
History
Present-day Botswana was primarily forest ten million years ago.
[
17
]
Homo erectus
lived in the region during the
Early Stone Age
.
[
18
]
Stone tools in present-day Botswana, date back to two million years ago.
[
19
]
[
20
]
Hominin migration to the
Kalahari Desert
, which includes Botswana, is estimated to have happened prior to 186,000 years ago.
[
20
]
Lake Makgadikgadi began to shrink approximately 50,000 years ago.
[
21
]
Roughly 30,000–40,000 years ago, the ancestors of the
Khoe
and the
San
lived in the region, adapting their movements to changing water and climate conditions.
[
22
]
Rock art
dates back to approximately 30,000 years ago,
[
23
]
and permanent water sources were widely inhabited by 20,000 years ago.
[
24
]
Around 2,000 years ago, people introduced cattle, sheep, pottery, and
agriculture
.
[
25
]
Crops included
millet
,
sorghum
,
cowpeas
, and more.
[
26
]
Bantu-speaking peoples migrated
into the region between 2,000 and 1,500 years ago;
[
27
]
the
Kalanga
arrived around 200 CE and ancestors of the
Tswana
c.
400 CE
[
28
]
who introduced iron and copper tools along with establishing permanent settlements.
[
29
]
From the 7th century, trade expanded,
[
30
]
[
31
]
connecting Botswana with wider
southern Africa
and eventually the
Indian Ocean trade
.
[
31
]
The Toutswe people, the
Kingdom of Mapungubwe
, and later
Great Zimbabwe
became important regional powers,
[
32
]
[
33
]
with cattle and gold playing major economic roles.
[
34
]
[
35
]
[
36
]
From the 15th to 18th centuries, Tswana and Kalanga peoples migrated and formed new political communities.
[
37
]
[
38
]
Tswana society became organized into
merafe
(plural form of
morafe
), a type of tribal government ruled by chiefs known as
dikgosi
(plural form of
kgosi
),
[
39
]
while cattle became a major asset to the region.
[
40
]
[
37
]
The
Difaqane
of the late 18th and early 19th century caused widespread warfare and migration,
[
41
]
[
42
]
[
43
]
which strengthened Tswana settlement across present-day Botswana.
[
42
]
By the 1840s, many states had been re-established and governed through the
kgotla
, a traditional community council.
[
44
]
[
45
]
European influence expanded after missionaries arrived in 1816,
[
46
]
followed by British traders and explorers.
[
46
]
[
47
]
David Livingstone established a mission in 1845, while Christianity and European trade spread.
[
48
]
Conflict with Boer forces continued,
[
49
]
and the discovery of the
Tati Goldfields
in 1868 led to a gold rush and the growth of
Francistown
as a major mining and railway centre.
[
46
]
[
50
]
In 1852, a coalition of
Tswana
chiefdoms led by
Sechele I
[
51
]
defeated Afrikaner incursions at the
Battle of Dimawe
and, after about eight years of intermittent tensions and hostilities, eventually came to a peace agreement in
Potchefstroom
in 1860.
[
52
]
In 1884,
Batawana
, a northern-based Tswana clan's cavalry under the command of
kgosi
Moremi II, fought and defeated the Ndebele's invasion of northern Botswana at the Battle of Khutiyabasadi.
[
53
]
This was the start of the collapse of the
Ndebele kingdom
in Zimbabwe, helping Tswana speaking authority.
[
53
]
In 1885, Britain established the
Bechuanaland Protectorate
to prevent
German
and
Afrikaner expansion
while maintaining a strategic link between southern and
central Africa
.
[
54
]
[
55
]
[
56
]
[
57
]
Tswana
dikgosi
supported British protection since they feared
settler colonialism
by Germany along with incorporation into South Africa and the mining magnate
Cecil Rhodes
.
[
58
]
[
59
]
The protectorate was divided into tribal reserves and British crown land, with eight Tswana groups being recognized.
[
60
]
The
dikgosi
still had considerable authority, while Britain exercised relatively limited direct control, believing the protectorate would be absorbed by a British colony.
[
61
]
[
45
]
The territory was economically dependent on South Africa.
[
62
]
[
59
]
In 1895,
Khama III, Sebele I, and Bathoen I travelled to Britain
and successfully persuaded the British government not to transfer the protectorate to Cecil Rhodes's
British South Africa Company
.
[
63
]
[
64
]
[
54
]
This mission became an important early example of Tswana political unity.
[
65
]
[
66
]
The protectorate suffered heavily from the
rinderpest epidemic of the 1890s
, losing livestock and wild game.
[
64
]
Britain introduced
hut
and
poll taxes
,
[
67
]
and the protectorate joined the
South African Customs Union
in 1910.
[
64
]
At this point, all Tswana tribes had adopted
Christianity
.
[
46
]
During the
First World War
, hundreds of Batswana served with
British forces
.
[
68
]
British involvement increased during the 1930s,
[
69
]
[
70
]
as the administration sought to develop the cattle economy while imposing greater controls on the
dikgosi
.
[
70
]
[
61
]
[
64
]
A severe drought earlier in the decade had killed much of the protectorate's cattle.
[
71
]
Bechuanaland sent roughly 11,000 men to serve alongside
British forces during the Second World War
,
[
72
]
with most serving in the British Army's
African Auxiliary Pioneer Corps
.
[
73
]
The war brought shortages, higher prices, taxation, and economic disruption throughout the protectorate;
[
74
]
however, relative to other nations in the British Empire, the people of Bechuanaland approved of the war.
[
75
]
Following the war; education, wage labour, and civic organizations contributed to the emergence of a new political class that increasingly challenged traditional chiefly authority.
[
76
]
[
77
]
The most important political crisis came from
Seretse Khama
, heir to the
Ngwato
chieftainship, whose marriage to the British white woman
Ruth Williams
caused controversy.
[
78
]
[
79
]
In 1950, Britain banished the couple from the protectorate under pressure from South Africa and racial politics surrounding
apartheid
.
[
61
]
Seretse's supporters protested,
[
80
]
[
81
]
and he was eventually allowed to return in 1956.
[
81
]
The controversy weakened the authority of the chiefs and strengthened the movement toward representative government.
[
82
]
Political parties emerged, including the
Bechuanaland People's Party
in 1960
[
83
]
and Seretse Khama's
Bechuanaland Democratic Party
(BDP) in 1962.
[
84
]
A new system reduced the political power of chiefs while preserving them in a
Ntlo ya Dikgosi
(House of Chiefs).
[
85
]
Gaborone became the capital in 1965,
[
84
]
and the protectorate gained self-government.
[
86
]
The BDP won the
first general election
, and on 30 September 1966,
[
86
]
[
87
]
the Bechuanaland Protectorate became the independent Republic of Botswana, with Seretse Khama as its first
president
.
[
86
]
[
87
]
Botswana
gained independence in 1966
and established a
liberal democracy
based on elections, human rights, and a
Westminster system
with Seretse Khama as its first president.
[
86
]
[
87
]
Traditional chiefs and institutions such as the
kgotla
were retained but placed under the national legal system.
[
88
]
[
89
]
[
44
]
[
90
]
[
91
]
Botswana was extremely poor at independence, with low literacy, little infrastructure, and an economy heavily dependent on cattle farming and South Africa.
[
92
]
[
93
]
[
94
]
Under Seretse Khama
, the government invested in roads, schools, and other public services.
[
95
]
[
96
]
[
97
]
The discovery of diamonds in 1967 transformed the economy.
[
98
]
[
99
]
[
100
]
Partnerships with
De Beers
and the creation of
Debswana
allowed the government to gain substantial diamond revenue, helping Botswana become one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
[
101
]
[
102
]
After Seretse Khama's death in 1980, then
Vice-President of Botswana
Quett Masire
became the president of Botswana.
[
103
]
Quett Masire continued Khama's development policies, preserving faith in the government.
[
104
]
Strong opposition of the Botswana Democratic Party started gaining traction in the 1890s, with many opposition parties winning local elections.
[
105
]
Previously dependent on support by specific ethnic groups, the
Botswana National Front
gained support among the working class.
[
106
]
By the
1984 general election
, it was a competitive opposition party.
[
107
]
HIV/AIDS
had caused the
life expectancy
to drop from 67 to 50 years in one decade.
[
108
]
[
109
]
Festus Mogae
became president in 1998 when Quett Masire stepped down as President.
[
110
]
Mogae continued economic development and made HIV/AIDS treatment a major priority.
[
111
]
[
112
]
The
Botswana–Namibia border
came under dispute in 1999 when both countries claimed the
Sedudu Island
.
[
113
]
[
114
]
The dispute went to the International Court of Justice
, where it was ruled that the island belonged to Botswana.
[
114
]
The San people issued a legal challenge in 2002 to contest their expulsion from the
Central Kalahari Game Reserve
, but the case was dismissed.
[
115
]
Ian Khama
, the son of
Seretse Khama
succeeded to the presidency at the end of Mogae's term on 1 April 2008.
[
116
]
His style of leadership was advertised as following the "four Ds": democracy, development, dignity, and discipline.
[
117
]
Khama centralised power around the presidency.
[
118
]
The
2008 financial crisis
pressured Botswana's economy, which remained dependent on diamond mines despite the government's efforts.
[
119
]
The diamond industry ended a steady decline when it stabilised at about 39% of the nation's GDP in 2009.
[
99
]
The BDP retained its majority in the legislature after the
2014 general election
, but for the first time it did so with only a plurality of the popular vote.
[
120
]
Ian Khama then appointed Masisi as his vice-president.
[
121
]
The decision was controversial because of Masisi's inexperience relative to other possible choices.
[
122
]
Following the
2019 general election
,
Mokgweetsi Masisi
was elected president.
[
123
]
He reversed several Khama-era policies and pursued anti-corruption measures.
[
124
]
[
125
]
In the
2024 Botswana general election
, the opposition
Umbrella for Democratic Change
defeated the Botswana Democratic Party, ending 58 years of BDP rule and making
Duma Boko
president.
[
126
]
His government has emphasized economic diversification, including solar energy and technology, while also confronting a
major healthcare crisis
caused by shortages of medicines and supplies.
[
127
]
[
128
]
Geography
Botswana's geography features a predominantly flat and dry landscape, with much of the country covered by the
Kalahari Desert
.
[
129
]
The country's terrain consists of sandy soils, rocky hill ranges, grasslands, and more.
[
129
]
Much of Botswana's population is concentrated in the southeastern part of the country, where major urban centres are located.
[
130
]
Botswana is a landlocked country in
southern Africa
, bordered by
Namibia
to the west and north,
Zambia
to the north, Zimbabwe to the northeast, and
South Africa
to the south and southeast.
[
131
]
Botswana features the
Okavango Delta
located in the northwest, a vast inland river delta where the
Okavango River
spreads across the Kalahari rather than flowing into the sea.
[
129
]
[
132
]
The delta contains numerous channels, lagoons, islands, and seasonal wetlands and supports wildlife.
[
132
]
The
Chobe River
in the north also forms part of Botswana's border with Namibia and contributes to the region's extensive wetlands.
[
129
]
Botswana's climate
is generally semi-arid.
[
129
]
Rainfall is highly seasonal and varies considerably across the country.
[
129
]
The northern and eastern areas generally receive more rainfall than the dry southwest.
[
129
]
Summers can be extremely hot, while winter nights can become quite cold.
[
133
]
Botswana is vulnerable to several natural and environmental hazards.
[
134
]
Drought is a recurring environmental challenge and can have significant effects on agriculture, livestock, water supplies, and wildlife.
[
129
]
[
135
]
Periods of heavy rainfall can also cause localized flooding, particularly in the Okavango and Chobe regions and along seasonal waterways.
[
134
]
Veldfires
typically occur during the winter dry season.
[
134
]
These fires are either natural, which are triggered by lightning during the rainy season, or unnatural, which are caused by human intervention during the dry season and often prolonged by delayed rainfall.
[
134
]
Botswana has a high biodiversity, particularly in the
Okavango Delta
, featuring thousands of plant and animal species including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish.
[
136
]
[
137
]
However, critical data gaps regarding species distribution and status significantly hinder conservation efforts.
[
137
]
The country features many
protected areas
allowing large areas of natural habitat to remain intact.
[
138
]
Botswana has some of the largest and most important
wildlife populations in Africa
.
[
138
]
Wildlife is particularly concentrated in the north since
wetlands
and
savannas
in the area provide permanent or seasonal sources of water.
[
129
]
[
139
]
Northern Botswana has one of the few remaining large populations of the endangered
African wild dog
.
[
140
]
Since raising livestock has been profitable for the people of Botswana, land continues to be exploited with dramatically increasing numbers of animals.
[
141
]
From 1966 to 1991, the livestock population grew from 1.7
million to 5.5
million.
[
141
]
Environmentalists report that the Okavango Delta is drying up due to increased livestock grazing.
[
142
]
The Okavango Delta is one of the major semi-forested wetlands in Botswana and one of the largest inland deltas in the world; the ecosystem is crucial to the survival of many animals.
[
142
]
Botswana faces two major
environmental
problems, drought and
desertification
, which are heavily linked. Three-quarters of the country's human and animal populations depend on groundwater due to drought.
[
141
]
Groundwater
use through deep borehole drilling has somewhat eased the effects of drought. Surface water is scarce in Botswana, and less than 5% of the agriculture in the country is sustainable by rainfall.
[
141
]
In the remaining 95% of the country, raising livestock is the primary source of rural income.
[
141
]
Approximately 71% of the country's land is used for communal grazing, which has been a major cause of the desertification and the accelerating soil erosion in the country.
[
141
]
Botswana had a 2018
Forest Landscape Integrity Index
mean score of 9.13/10, ranking it 8th globally out of 172 countries.
[
143
]
Government and politics
Botswana is a
parliamentary republic
governed by the
Constitution of Botswana
.
[
144
]
It is the longest uninterrupted democracy in Africa.
[
145
]
Its seat of government is in
Gaborone
.
[
146
]
Botswana's governing institutions were established after it became an independent nation in 1966.
[
144
]
Botswana's governmental structure is based on both the United Kingdom's
Westminster system
and the Tswana people's tribal governments.
[
144
]
Botswana has a
centralised government
in which national law supersedes local law.
[
147
]
Local laws are developed by local councils and district councils.
[
148
]
They are heavily influenced by tribal governments, which are led by the tribe's chief.
[
148
]
The
Parliament of Botswana
consists of the President and the
National Assembly
, which serves as the nation's formal and sole legislature, while the
Ntlo ya Dikgosi
serves an advisory body made up of tribal chiefs and other appointed members.
[
149
]
Botswana's executive branch is led by the
President of Botswana
, who serves as both the
head of state
and
head of government
.
[
144
]
The members of parliament choose the president,
[
150
]
and the president then appoints the
vice-president
and
cabinet
members.
[
151
]
The president has significant power in Botswana, and the legislature has little power to
check
the president once appointed.
[
150
]
[
152
]
The judiciary includes the
High Court of Botswana
, the Court of Appeal and Magistrates' Courts.
[
153
]
Cases are often settled by customary courts with tribal chiefs presiding.
[
148
]
Elections in Botswana
are held every five years and overseen by the
Independent Electoral Commission
(IEC).
[
154
]
Botswana operates a
multi-party system
in which
many political parties
compete in elections.
[
145
]
It was a
dominant-party
state in which the
Botswana Democratic Party
had ruled with a majority government from independence in 1966 to 2024.
[
155
]
[
84
]
The nation's elections are recognised as
free and fair
, but the ruling party has institutional advantages that other parties do not.
[
154
]
[
156
]
Factionalism
is common within Botswana's political parties, and several groups have formed new parties by splitting from established ones.
[
145
]
Since 2019, the
Umbrella for Democratic Change
has operated as a coalition of opposition parties.
[
157
]
The most recent election was held
in 2024
, with the Botswana Democratic Party losing its majority for the first time in history, ending its 58-year rule over the country. The election saw
Duma Boko
being elected as president.
[
158
]
In Botswana's early years, its politics were managed by President
Seretse Khama
and vice-president (later president)
Quett Masire
.
[
159
]
Since the
Kgabo Commission
in 1991, factionalism and political rivalries have dominated Botswana politics. The
Barata-Phathi
faction was led by
Peter Mmusi
,
Daniel Kwelagobe
and
Ponatshego Kedikilwe
, while the A Team faction was led by
Mompati Merafhe
and Jacob Nkate.
[
160
]
[
161
]
When
Festus Mogae
and
Ian Khama
became president and vice-president, respectively, they aligned with the A Team. Khama effectively expelled the A Team from the party in 2010 after he became president.
[
161
]
A new rivalry formed in 2018 when Khama's chosen successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi, became president. He opposed Khama, and the two formed a political rivalry that continues to loom over Botswana politics in the 2020s.
[
162
]
Botswana was ranked as a "flawed democracy" and 33rd out of 167 states in the 2023
Democracy Index (The Economist)
, which was the second-highest rating in Africa, and the highest ranking in continental Africa (only the offshore island nation of
Mauritius
bested its ranking).
[
163
]
However, according to the 2024
V-Dem Democracy Indices
, Botswana has been experiencing an episode of
democratic backsliding
over the past 10 years, recording its lowest ever score on the indices.
[
164
]
The 2025
Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index
ranked Botswana as the third-least corrupt country in Africa, just below
Cape Verde
and the
Seychelles
.
[
165
]
At the time of independence, Botswana had no armed forces. It was only after the
Rhodesian
and
South African armies
attacked the
Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army
and
Umkhonto we Sizwe
[
166
]
bases respectively that the
Botswana Defence Force
(BDF) was formed in 1977.
[
167
]
The president is
commander-in-chief
of the armed forces and appoints a defence council. In 2019, Botswana signed the UN
treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
.
[
168
]
Following political changes in South Africa and the region, the BDF's missions have increasingly focused on preventing
poaching
,
preparing for disasters
, and supporting foreign
peacekeeping
. The United States has been the largest single foreign contributor to the development of the
BDF
, and a large segment of its officer corps have received US training. The Botswana government gave the United States permission to explore the possibility of establishing an Africa Command (
AFRICOM
) base in the country.
[
169
]
Botswana is the 50th most peaceful country in the world, according to the 2024
Global Peace Index
.
[
170
]
Botswana is a member of the
Commonwealth of Nations
.
[
171
]
Freedom House considers Botswana to be free with a score of 72/100 in its 2022
Freedom in the World
report. It scored high in political rights, though Freedom House expressed concerns regarding the representation of women and minorities and the lack of
freedom of information laws
. It also scored high in civil rights, though Freedom House expressed concerns regarding
freedom of the press
and the
right to strike
.
[
172
]
Transparency International
has regularly recognised Botswana as the least corrupt country in Africa,
[
173
]
and it is often described as comparable to the liberal democracies of Western Europe.
[
174
]
One potential issues for human rights in Botswana is the lack of strong checks and balances in the government, which allows the president to exercise wide latitude over policy and arbitrarily curtail free speech.
[
175
]
Early focus on
public works
projects after Botswana's independence rather than militarisation is credited for early legitimacy of the government, permitting stability in the nation's politics.
[
176
]
Conceptions of human rights in Botswana are shaped by collectivist traditions such as
botho
philosophy
rather than individualist traditions. Confrontational approaches to human rights such as
protest
,
strike action
and public condemnation are often seen as uncivil foreign inventions. Activism in Botswana instead focuses mainly on providing goods and services to those in need. Human rights
Non-governmental organisations
are relatively uncommon in Botswana. Among the most active is the Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS, which emphasises response to HIV but also addresses other areas such as the rights of women, children and LGBT people.
[
177
]
Many of the indigenous
San people

Since independence, Botswana has had one of the fastest growth rates in per capita income in the world.
[
186
]
Formerly one of the world's poorest countries—with a GDP per capita of about US$70 per year in the late 1960s
[
187
]
—Botswana has transformed itself into an upper middle-income country. GDP per capita grew from $439 in 1950 to $15,842 in 2018.
[
188

Although Botswana was resource-abundant, a good institutional framework allowed the country to reinvest resource-income to generate stable future income.

in Africa, giving it a relatively high standard of living in Africa, around that of Mexico.
